title: 010 — GitHub package firewall: an install-time gate for npm
html:
010 — GitHub package firewall: an install-time gate for npm

The one idea: GitHub's package firewall (public preview) sits between your machines and the npm registry. It checks every package lookup and download against your policy before anything installs. It's aimed at attacks that run during install, and at coding agents and CI runners that install dependencies with no human watching.

Added 2026-10-26 · Announced 2026-10-20 by GitHub

1. What it is

Item Detail
Status Public preview, free during the preview, metered billing (like Actions) at GA
Who GitHub Enterprise Cloud customers, including data residency
Ecosystem npm only for now
Where it sits Between endpoints (developer machines, coding agents, CI/CD hosts) or internal registries, and the upstream npm registry
What it checks Package metadata requests and package downloads
Policy controls A cooldown period for new versions, GitHub Advisory Database malware and vulnerability advisories, and supply-chain checks such as attestation downgrades
False positives The blocked-install error links to a form for requesting an exception

2. Why it matters

  • Malicious code can run before you look at it. An npm package's postinstall script runs during npm install. A compromised version can steal tokens from a CI runner before any scan of your code happens.
  • Agents install without asking. Coding agents add and install packages on their own. A gate at the network level protects them the same way it protects people.
  • A cooldown blocks brand-new versions. Many recent attacks published a malicious version and were caught within hours. A policy that refuses versions younger than a few days avoids most of them.
  • Angular front ends are npm. Even a .NET team has an npm supply chain if it ships Angular.

3. How it works

---
title: Package firewall in the install path
---
flowchart LR
    A["Developer, CI runner<br/>or coding agent"] -->|"npm install"| F["GitHub package firewall"]
    F -->|"check policy:<br/>advisories, cooldown, attestations"| P{"Allowed?"}
    P -->|"yes"| U["npm registry"]
    U --> F --> A
    P -->|"no"| B["Install fails<br/>with exception-request link"]

Clients point at the firewall instead of the public registry. The firewall evaluates each metadata request and download, passes allowed packages through, and blocks the rest with an error that explains the decision.

4. How to use it

Follow "Protecting endpoints with package firewall" in the GitHub Enterprise Cloud docs. The steps in outline:

  1. An enterprise admin enables the firewall and sets the policy: cooldown, advisory checks and attestation checks.
  2. Point npm clients at the firewall. On CI runners and agent environments, that means the registry setting in .npmrc or the runner image.
  3. Keep a short path for exception requests, so a false positive doesn't stall a release.

In practice:

  • Start with CI runners and agent sandboxes. They install the most and are watched the least.
  • Combine the firewall with lockfiles (package-lock.json) and npm ci, so builds install only what was reviewed.
  • Keep scanning with Dependabot as well. The firewall stops bad installs, and Dependabot tells you about bad packages you already have.

5. Trade-offs and limits

  • npm only. NuGet, PyPI and Maven aren't covered yet. For NuGet, keep using package source mapping and a curated feed such as Azure Artifacts upstreams.
  • Preview. Features and setup may change, and costs will be metered at GA.
  • Enterprise Cloud only. Free and Team plans can't use it.
  • A cooldown slows urgent upgrades. You'll need the exception path for real zero-day fixes.
  • Adopt now or wait? If you're on Enterprise Cloud, pilot it on CI now while it's free. Everyone else should get the same benefits from npm ci, lockfiles and a curated internal registry.

6. Where it fits

  • GitHub: Actions lockfiles, AI Scan and agentic autofix: the Actions side of the same supply-chain push.
  • Security engineering: supply-chain attacks and defence in depth.
  • CI/CD fundamentals: where dependency installation happens in a pipeline.
  • Angular and TypeScript deep dive: the npm toolchain behind an Angular app.

7. Questions to test yourself

  1. Why is install time a good moment for an attacker, especially on a CI runner?
  2. How does a cooldown period reduce risk, and what does it cost you?
  3. What does the firewall stop that Dependabot alerts don't?
  4. What would you use today to protect a NuGet supply chain in the same way?
  5. Why do coding agents raise the stakes for install-time attacks?

Sources

  • GitHub package firewall in public preview — GitHub Changelog, 20 Oct 2026
